MOVBYTS.description:
Rearranges the bytes of a 32-bit value according to a quaternary pattern. Each 
digit in the pattern (0-3) specifies which source byte maps to that destination 
position. This is the Spin2 function version of the PASM2 MOVBYTS instruction.
Available in PNut/pnut_ts v52 and later compilers. No version directive required.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: 32-bit value whose bytes will be rearranged

parameters.name: order
parameters.description: Quaternary pattern specifying byte arrangement (%%3210 format)

returns.description: Value with bytes rearranged per pattern

examples.code:
' Reverse byte order - no version directive needed, just v52+ compiler
PUB reverse_bytes(value) : result
  result := MOVBYTS(value, %%0123)
  ' $12_34_56_78 becomes $78_56_34_12

' Broadcast lowest byte to all positions
PUB broadcast_low(value) : result
  result := MOVBYTS(value, %%0000)
  ' $12_34_56_78 becomes $78_78_78_78

' Swap word-aligned byte pairs
PUB swap_pairs(value) : result
  result := MOVBYTS(value, %%1032)
  ' $12_34_56_78 becomes $34_12_78_56

' Extract and replicate specific byte
PUB replicate_byte(value, which) : result
  case which
    0: result := MOVBYTS(value, %%0000)
    1: result := MOVBYTS(value, %%1111)
    2: result := MOVBYTS(value, %%2222)
    3: result := MOVBYTS(value, %%3333)
examples.description: Replicate any byte to all positions

notes: Available in v52+ compilers - no version directive required
Pattern uses quaternary (base-4) notation with %% prefix
Each digit specifies source byte for that position
Digit 0 = lowest byte, digit 3 = highest byte
More flexible than ENDIANL/ENDIANW for custom patterns
Maps to PASM2 MOVBYTS instruction
MOVBYTS.oneliner: Rearrange bytes by quaternary pattern (v52+ compiler)

EXP.description:
Computes e (Euler's number ≈ 2.71828) raised to the power of a floating-point 
exponent (e^x). Computed internally as EXP2(x / ln(2)). Returns the natural 
antilogarithm, essential for exponential growth/decay calculations.
REQUIRES: {Spin2_v51} or later version directive at start of source file.

parameters.name: float_exponent
parameters.description: Exponent value (IEEE 754 single precision)

examples.code:
{Spin2_v51}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB main() | result
  result := EXP(1.0)                     ' result ≈ 2.71828 (e^1 = e)

{Spin2_v51}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB exp_examples() | result
  result := EXP(0.0)                     ' result = 1.0 (e^0)
  result := EXP(-1.0)                    ' result ≈ 0.36788 (1/e)
  result := EXP(2.0)                     ' result ≈ 7.389 (e^2)
  result := EXP(-2.0)                    ' result ≈ 0.1353 (e^-2)

{Spin2_v51}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB exponential_decay(initial, decay_rate, time) : remaining
  ' N(t) = N0 * e^(-λt)
  remaining := initial *. EXP(-decay_rate *. time)

{Spin2_v51}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB continuous_compound(principal, rate, time) : final
  ' A = P * e^(rt) - continuous compound interest
  final := principal *. EXP(rate *. time)

{Spin2_v51}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB gaussian(x, mean, stddev) : probability
  ' Normal distribution probability density
  ' f(x) = (1/(σ√(2π))) * e^(-((x-μ)²)/(2σ²))
  probability := EXP(-0.5 *. ((x -. mean) /. stddev) *. ((x -. mean) /. stddev))
  probability := probability /. (stddev *. 2.506628)  ' stddev * √(2π)

notes: REQUIRES {Spin2_v51} or later at start of source file
Computed as EXP2(x / ln(2)) internally
Returns NaN for extreme exponents (overflow/underflow)
Essential for exponential growth/decay models
Inverse of LOG() function
e ≈ 2.718281828 (Euler's number)
EXP.oneliner: Compute e^x (natural exponential) for floating-point exponent (requires Spin2_v51)

EXP2.description:
Computes 2 raised to the power of a floating-point exponent (2^x). Uses the 
hardware CORDIC QEXP instruction internally for efficient computation. Returns 
the antilogarithm base 2.
REQUIRES: {Spin2_v51} or later version directive at start of source file.

parameters.name: float_exponent
parameters.description: Exponent value (IEEE 754 single precision)

examples.code:
{Spin2_v51}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB main() | result
  result := EXP2(3.0)                    ' result = 8.0 (2^3)

{Spin2_v51}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB exp2_examples() | result
  result := EXP2(0.0)                    ' result = 1.0 (2^0)
  result := EXP2(1.0)                    ' result = 2.0 (2^1)
  result := EXP2(-1.0)                   ' result = 0.5 (2^-1)
  result := EXP2(0.5)                    ' result ≈ 1.414 (√2)
  result := EXP2(10.0)                   ' result = 1024.0 (2^10)

{Spin2_v51}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB binary_scale(value, shift) : scaled
  ' Scale value by power of 2 (like bit shifting but for floats)
  scaled := value *. EXP2(FLOAT(shift))

{Spin2_v51}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB octave_to_freq(octave, semitone) : freq
  ' Calculate frequency from octave and semitone
  ' A4 (octave 4, semitone 0) = 440Hz
  freq := 440.0 *. EXP2(FLOAT(octave - 4) +. FLOAT(semitone) /. 12.0)

notes: REQUIRES {Spin2_v51} or later at start of source file
Uses hardware CORDIC QEXP instruction internally
Returns NaN for extreme exponents (overflow/underflow)
Useful for binary scaling and DSP applications
Inverse of LOG2() function
More efficient than general POW for powers of 2

PUB init_table()
  BYTEFILL(@lookup, $FF, 256)  ' All entries invalid
  ' Then set specific valid entries
  lookup[10] := 1
  lookup[20] := 2

' Create test pattern
VAR
  BYTE pattern[1000]
  
PUB create_pattern()
  BYTEFILL(@pattern[0], $AA, 500)
  BYTEFILL(@pattern[500], $55, 500)

performance_comparison.manual_loop:
' Slower for large counts
REPEAT i FROM 0 TO count-1
  BYTE[dest][i] := value
performance_comparison.bytefill:
' Optimized implementation
BYTEFILL(dest, value, count)
' 3-10x faster for count > 10

notes: Only uses lower 8 bits of value
Count of 0 is safe (no operation)
No bounds checking on addresses
Cannot fill cog or LUT RAM
Sequential fill only
best_practices: Use appropriate fill value for data type

LOG2.description:
Computes the base-2 logarithm of a floating-point value. Returns the exponent 
that 2 must be raised to in order to produce the input value (2^result = input).
Uses the CORDIC QLOG instruction internally for efficient computation.
REQUIRES: {Spin2_v51} or later version directive at start of source file.

parameters.name: float_value
parameters.description: Positive floating-point number (IEEE 754 single precision)

examples.code:
{Spin2_v51}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB main() | x, result
  x := 8.0
  result := LOG2(x)                      ' result = 3.0 (2^3 = 8)

{Spin2_v51}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB log_examples() | result
  result := LOG2(1.0)                    ' result = 0.0 (2^0 = 1)
  result := LOG2(2.0)                    ' result = 1.0 (2^1 = 2)
  result := LOG2(4.0)                    ' result = 2.0 (2^2 = 4)
  result := LOG2(0.5)                    ' result = -1.0 (2^-1 = 0.5)

{Spin2_v51}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB bits_needed(max_value) : bits
  ' Calculate minimum bits needed to represent a value
  if max_value > 0.0
    bits := TRUNC(LOG2(max_value)) + 1
  else
    bits := 1
examples.description: Calculate bits needed for a value

examples.code:
{Spin2_v51}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB octave_from_freq(freq) : octave
  ' Calculate musical octave from frequency (A4 = 440Hz)
  octave := TRUNC(LOG2(freq / 440.0)) + 4

notes: REQUIRES {Spin2_v51} or later at start of source file
Returns NaN if input is negative or zero
Uses hardware CORDIC QLOG instruction internally
Input must be IEEE 754 single-precision float
Result is IEEE 754 single-precision float
Inverse of EXP2() function
LOG2.oneliner: Base-2 logarithm of floating-point value (requires Spin2_v51)

PINLOW.description:
Drive specified pin(s) low (output mode, logic 0).
Sets the direction bit(s) to output (DIR=1) and drives the pin(s) low (OUT=0).
This is equivalent to the PASM2 DIRL instruction.

parameters.name: PinField
parameters.description:
Specifies which pin(s) to drive low. Can be:
- Single pin number (0-63)
- Pin range using '..' operator (Bottom..Top)
- Multiple pins using ADDPINS operator
- Variable or expression that evaluates to a pin field

timing.hub_access: 8-19 clock cycles when executed from hub

examples.code: PINLOW(56)
PINLOW(0 ADDPINS 7)
PINLOW(49..40)
examples.description: Drive pins 40 through 49 low (wraps if needed)

examples.code:
VAR
  LONG led_pin
PUB main()
  led_pin := 56
  PINLOW(led_pin)
examples.description: Use a variable for the pin number

underlying_pasm.description: Internally uses DIRL instruction which sets DIR=1 and OUT=0

related_methods: PINWRITE - Write specific value to pins
notes: Pin becomes an output if it wasn't already
Overrides any smart pin mode on the pin
Pin will remain low until explicitly changed
Multiple pins can be controlled simultaneously
Useful for Charlieplexing one side of LED matrix

MULDIV64.description: Multiply then divide with 64-bit intermediate result

parameters.name: Multiplier
parameters.description: First value to multiply (32-bit signed)

parameters.name: Multiplicand
parameters.description: Second value to multiply (32-bit signed)

parameters.name: Divisor
parameters.description: Value to divide by (32-bit signed, non-zero)

examples.code:
' Scale value without overflow

' Calculate percentage

notes: Prevents overflow in intermediate calculation
Uses 64-bit intermediate result
All parameters are 32-bit signed
Division by zero returns 0
Useful for scaling and ratio calculations
More precise than (a*b)/c for large values

POLLCT.description: Check if system counter has passed specified tick value

parameters.name: Tick
parameters.description: 32-bit system counter target value to check

returns.description: TRUE (-1) if tick has passed, FALSE (0) if not yet

examples.code:
' Non-blocking timeout check
timeout := GETCT() + clkfreq  ' 1 second timeout
repeat
  ' Do work...
  if POLLCT(timeout)
    ' Timeout occurred
    quit

' Check if delay has elapsed
start_time := GETCT()
end_time := start_time + clkfreq/10
repeat while not POLLCT(end_time)
  ' Do other work while waiting

' Multiple timer management
repeat
  if POLLCT(timer1)
    handle_timer1()
    timer1 += period1
  if POLLCT(timer2)
    handle_timer2()
    timer2 += period2

notes: Non-blocking alternative to WAITCT
Returns immediately with TRUE/FALSE result
Handles counter wraparound correctly
Useful for implementing timeouts
Can check multiple timers in same loop
TRUE means current counter >= target (accounting for wrap)

parameters.description: Destination buffer address

Prevents buffer overflow

LOCKNEW.description: Allocate a new hardware lock for inter-cog synchronization

returns.description: Lock ID (0..15) if successful, negative if no locks available

examples.code:
' Allocate a new lock
lock := LOCKNEW()
if lock < 0
  ' No locks available
  abort

VAR
  long buffer_lock

PUB init()
  buffer_lock := LOCKNEW()

' Multiple locks for different resources

uart_lock := LOCKNEW()
i2c_lock := LOCKNEW()

notes: P2 has 16 hardware locks (0-15)
Returns next available lock ID
Returns negative value if all locks in use
Lock is marked as allocated but not captured
Must call LOCKRET when done to free lock

QCOS.description: Calculate cosine of angle using hardware CORDIC

parameters.name: Angle
parameters.description: Angle in P2 angle units (0..$FFFFFFFF = 0..360°)

parameters.name: Length
parameters.description: Hypotenuse/radius length (scaling factor)

' Calculate cosine of 60 degrees

' Result: cosine ≈ 500

  plot(x++, center_y + y)

' Horizontal position for circular motion

notes: Uses P2's hardware CORDIC engine
Result = Length × cos(Angle)
Full 32-bit precision

Handles all quadrants correctly

TASKHLT.description:
The TASKHLT register holds the halt status bits for all 32 tasks in the current 
cog. Each bit corresponds to a task ID (0-31), where a set bit indicates that 
task is currently halted. Note that the bits are stored in reverse order - bit 0 
corresponds to task 31, and bit 31 corresponds to task 0.
REQUIRES: {Spin2_v47} or later version directive at start of source file.

examples.code:
{Spin2_v47}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB check_task_halted(task_id) : halted
  ' Note: bits are reversed - task 0 is bit 31, task 31 is bit 0
  halted := (TASKHLT >> (31 - task_id)) & 1
examples.description: Check if a specific task is halted

examples.code:
{Spin2_v47}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB count_halted_tasks() : count | i
  count := 0
  repeat i from 0 to 31
    if (TASKHLT >> (31 - i)) & 1
      count++

{Spin2_v47}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB any_tasks_halted() : result
  result := TASKHLT <> 0
examples.description: Quick check if any tasks are halted

examples.code:
{Spin2_v47}                              ' REQUIRED directive
PUB monitor_tasks() | status
  repeat
    status := TASKHLT
    if status
      debug("Halted tasks: ", ubin(status))
    waitms(100)

notes: REQUIRES {Spin2_v47} or later at start of source file
Bits are stored in REVERSE order (bit 0 = task 31, bit 31 = task 0)
A set bit (1) indicates the task is halted
A clear bit (0) indicates the task is running or stopped
Task 0 is typically the main program task
Use TASKCHK() for simpler status checking of individual tasks
Direct TASKHLT access useful for bulk task monitoring
Writing to TASKHLT can force-halt or force-resume tasks
TASKHLT.oneliner: Register containing halt status bits for all 32 tasks (requires Spin2_v47)

unknown.description:
Communication registers PR0-PR7, shared between Spin2 and PASM2 code.

For PASM2 code that is either inline (within a Spin2 method) or called
by a Spin2 method, registers $1D8-$1DF are readable and writable by both
languages using the symbols PR0-PR7. This provides a communication
mechanism between Spin2 and PASM2 code running in the same COG.

IMPORTANT: PASM2 code launched into another COG does NOT share this
register space with Spin2. Each COG has its own independent PR0-PR7.

examples.name: Spin2 and inline PASM2 sharing registers
examples.code:
' Spin2 can read/write PR registers
PR0 := 100
value := PR1

' Inline PASM2 can access same registers
org
  mov   PR2, PR0           ' Copy PR0 to PR2
  add   PR0, #1            ' Increment PR0
end
examples.description: Both Spin2 and inline PASM2 access the same PR registers

notes: All 8 registers are functionally identical, differing only in address
NOT shared across COGs - each COG has independent copies
Located in COG RAM at addresses $1D8-$1DF
Available in both PASM2 and Spin2 syntax

ALIGNL.description: ALIGNL aligns the next data element to the beginning of the next long of Hub RAM. ALIGNL is important to use when code requires certain data to begin on a long boundary (for access convenience and speed). The directive causes up to three zero ($00) bytes to emit after the current data to automatically pad and align the next data element to a long boundary.
ALIGNL.category: Directive - Align to next long in Hub RAM
parameters: No parameters - This directive takes no arguments
ALIGNL.usage_notes:
ALIGNL is only allowed in DAT blocks, not in in-line PASM.

When data elements are naturally packed in memory, they may not align to convenient boundaries.
If code that accesses data expects it to align with a long boundary (for convenience or speed),
the ALIGNL directive achieves this by emitting 0-3 zero bytes as padding.

Note that elements after the ALIGNL are still packed right after each other, which may require
further alignment directives depending on the needs of the code accessing them.

examples.code:
DAT
  T1        BYTE $11
            ALIGNL          ' Pad to next long boundary
  T2        WORD $2222
            LONG $33333333
examples.comment: Aligns T2 to start at a long boundary by padding after T1

examples.code:
DAT
  Buffer    BYTE 0[13]      ' 13-byte buffer
            ALIGNL          ' Ensure next data is long-aligned
  LongData  LONG $12345678
examples.comment: Ensures LongData starts on a long boundary for faster access

FIT.description: Ensure code fits in specified limit
examples: FIT $1F0  // Must fit in COG space

ORGH.description:
Sets the origin address for hub RAM assembly code. In DAT blocks, ORGH positions 
code/data at a specific hub address. In V50+, ORGH also enables inline hub-execute 
assembly within Spin2 methods for performance-critical code sections.
ORGH.location: DAT block, or inline within PUB/PRI methods (V50+)

syntax.inline_spin2:
PUB/PRI method()
    ORGH
        ' Hub-execute PASM2 code
    END

parameters.name: address
parameters.description: Hub address for code/data placement (DAT block usage)

examples.code:
DAT
        orgh $400
data    long    0[16]                    ' 16 longs at hub address $400
examples.description: Basic hub address origin in DAT block

examples.code:
DAT
        orgh                              ' Continue from current hub address
table   long    100, 200, 300, 400
examples.description: ORGH without address continues from current location

examples.code:
DAT
        org                               ' Cog code
cog_routine
        mov     pa, #1
        ret

        orgh                              ' Switch to hub code
hub_data
        long    0[256]                    ' Large buffer in hub RAM
examples.description: Mixed cog and hub sections in DAT block

examples.code:
PUB fast_copy(src, dst, count) | i
  ORGH
        mov     ptrb, dst
        mov     ptra, src
        rep     @.end, count
        rdlong  i, ptra++
        wrlong  i, ptrb++
.end
  END
examples.description: V50+ inline hub-execute assembly in Spin2 method

examples.code:
PUB fast_fill(addr, value, count)
  ORGH
        mov     ptra, addr
        rep     @.end, count
        wrlong  value, ptra++
.end
  END
examples.description: V50+ inline assembly for fast memory fill

examples.code:
PUB compute_checksum(addr, bytes) : sum | temp
  sum := 0
  ORGH
        mov     ptra, addr
        mov     pr0, bytes
        mov     sum, #0
.loop
        rdbyte  temp, ptra++
        add     sum, temp
        djnz    pr0, #.loop
  END
examples.description: V50+ inline assembly with return value

inline_assembly.description:
V50+ feature: ORGH can be used within Spin2 methods to embed hub-execute
PASM2 code. The assembly runs in hub-execute mode directly in hub RAM.
features: Code executes in hub RAM (hub-execute mode)
Maximum size: $FFFF longs including auto-added RET
RET instruction automatically added at end
First 16 local variables saved/restored around inline block
Access to method parameters and local variables
error_messages: ORGH inline block exceeds $FFFF longs (including the added RET instruction)

restrictions: ORGH not allowed inside a DITTO block
Cannot use ORGH and ORG in same inline block
Inline blocks must end with END directive
notes: In DAT blocks, ORGH sets hub origin for subsequent code/data
Default address continues from current compilation position
V50+: ORGH enables inline hub-execute assembly in Spin2 methods
Hub-execute code runs in place, no cog RAM copy required
For inline blocks, ORG uses cog RAM, ORGH uses hub RAM
Choose ORG for speed-critical tiny routines, ORGH for larger code
ORGH.oneliner: Set hub RAM origin address; V50+ enables inline hub-execute assembly

DITTO.description:
Code/data replication directive that repeats a block of instructions or data a specified number of times.
The special $$ symbol provides the current iteration index (0 to count-1).
Requires Spin2 version 50 or later - must include {Spin2_v50} directive at file start.

examples.code:
{Spin2_v50}
DAT
        DITTO   4                   ' Repeat 4 times
        LONG    $77777777 + $$      ' Each long gets different value
        DITTO   END
examples.description: Data replication with iteration index - produces 4 LONGs with values $77777777, $77777778, $77777779, $7777777A

examples.code:
{Spin2_v50}
DAT
        ORG     0
        DITTO   8                   ' Repeat for 8 pins
        DRVH    #BasePin + $$       ' Drive pins BasePin+0 through BasePin+7
        DITTO   END

{Spin2_v50}
CON
  MotorCount = 4
DAT
        DITTO   MotorCount
        WYPIN   speed + $$, #BasePin + $$ * 2
        DITTO   END
examples.description: Using constants and expressions with iteration index

restrictions: ORG not allowed within a DITTO block
ORGH not allowed within a DITTO block
Block must end with DITTO END
DITTO.zero_count_behavior: When count is 0, block produces no output - completely skipped
notes: REQUIRES {Spin2_v50} or later version directive at start of source file
Works in both COG/LUT mode and ORGH (hub) mode
$$ evaluates to 0 on first iteration, count-1 on last
Compile-time replication - no runtime overhead
Useful for lookup tables, pin initialization, unrolled loops
DITTO.oneliner: Code/data replication directive with iteration index (requires Spin2_v50)

Include Binary File.name: Include Binary File
Include Binary File.description: Include the contents of an external binary file into Hub memory at assembly time
examples: datastart  FILE "config.dat"  ; Label the included data
Include Binary File.usage:
FILE is used in DAT sections to include the entire contents of an external
binary file directly into Hub memory. The file path is relative to the
source file location. This is useful for including images, fonts, lookup
tables, or other pre-compiled binary data. The data is inserted byte-for-byte
exactly as it appears in the file.
Include Binary File.alignment:
File data begins at the current assembly position without automatic alignment.
Use ALIGNL or ALIGNW before FILE if specific alignment is needed for the data.
limitations: File must exist at compile time

ALIGNW.description: ALIGNW aligns the next data element to the beginning of the next word of Hub RAM. ALIGNW is important to use when code requires certain data to begin on a word boundary (for access convenience and speed). The directive causes zero or one byte ($00) to emit after the current data to automatically pad and align the next data element to a word boundary.
ALIGNW.category: Directive - Align to next word in Hub RAM
parameters: No parameters - This directive takes no arguments
ALIGNW.usage_notes:
ALIGNW is only allowed in DAT blocks, not in in-line PASM.

When data elements are naturally packed in memory, they may not align to convenient boundaries.
If code that accesses data expects it to align with a word boundary (for convenience or speed),
the ALIGNW directive achieves this by emitting 0-1 zero bytes as padding.

Note that elements after the ALIGNW are still packed right after each other, which may require
further alignment directives depending on the needs of the code accessing them.

examples.code:
DAT
  T1        BYTE $11
            ALIGNW          ' Pad to next word boundary
  T2        WORD $2222
            LONG $33333333
examples.comment: Aligns T2 to start at a word boundary by padding after T1

examples.code:
DAT
  Buffer    BYTE 0[7]       ' 7-byte buffer
            ALIGNW          ' Ensure next data is word-aligned  
  WordData  WORD $1234
examples.comment: Ensures WordData starts on a word boundary for faster access

Insert Byte Data.name: Insert Byte Data
Insert Byte Data.description: Insert byte data into Hub memory at assembly time
Insert Byte Data.usage:
BYTE is used in DAT sections to define byte-sized data values that will
be stored in Hub memory. Multiple values can be specified separated by commas.
Strings are automatically converted to their byte values.
Insert Byte Data.alignment: Bytes are packed sequentially without padding

Insert Word Data.name: Insert Word Data
Insert Word Data.description: Insert word (16-bit) data into Hub memory at assembly time
Insert Word Data.usage:
WORD is used in DAT sections to define word-sized (16-bit) data values that
will be stored in Hub memory. Multiple values can be specified separated by
commas. Words are stored in little-endian format.
Insert Word Data.alignment:
Words may not be aligned unless preceded by ALIGNW. Using ALIGNW before
WORD data ensures proper word alignment for efficient access.

ORGF.description: Set origin address with forced alignment

Insert Long Data.name: Insert Long Data
Insert Long Data.description: Insert long (32-bit) data into Hub memory at assembly time
Insert Long Data.usage:
LONG is used in DAT sections to define long-sized (32-bit) data values that
will be stored in Hub memory. Multiple values can be specified separated by
commas. This is the native data size for P2 operations. Longs are stored
in little-endian format.
Insert Long Data.alignment:
Longs may not be aligned unless preceded by ALIGNL. Using ALIGNL before
LONG data ensures proper long alignment for efficient access and is
especially important for data that will be accessed as longs.

ORG.description: Set origin address for COG RAM

DEBUG.description:
Debug output statement for displaying values, text, and formatted data
during program execution. Supports multiple formatter methods and
display windows.
DEBUG.formatter_protocol:
Debug formatter methods follow a consistent underscore protocol:

WITHOUT UNDERSCORE (e.g., SDEC, UDEC, UHEX, UBIN):
  - Outputs variable name followed by equals sign and value
  - Example: DEBUG(SDEC(temperature)) outputs "temperature = -25"

WITH UNDERSCORE (e.g., SDEC_, UDEC_, UHEX_, UBIN_):
  - Outputs just the value without variable name
  - Example: DEBUG(SDEC_(temperature)) outputs "-25"
  - Useful for custom formatting or embedding values in strings

This protocol applies to all numeric formatters and their typed variants
(_BYTE, _WORD, _LONG suffixes).

..description: Decimal point or object method access

@@.description: Absolute address operator - get absolute hub address

^@.description: Object address operator - address within object

~.description: Post-clear operator - use value then clear
examples: value := ~flag  // use flag then clear it

$$.description:
The $$ symbol has dual meaning depending on context:

1. PASM2 CONTEXT: Current cog address - the address of the instruction where 
   $$ appears. Used for relative address calculations, jump offsets, and 
   position-independent code.

2. DITTO CONTEXT (V50+): Iteration index - inside a DITTO block, $$ equals
   the current iteration number (0 to count-1). Used for generating indexed
   sequences, lookup tables, and repetitive patterns.

pasm2_address.description: Current cog address in assembly code
pasm2_address.value: Address of current instruction (in cog longs)

ditto_index.description: Current iteration index in DITTO block

examples.code:
DAT
        org
        
routine mov     pa, #1
        jmp     #$$                        ' Jump to self (infinite loop)
examples.description: PASM2: $$ as current cog address for self-jump

examples.code:
DAT
        org
        
table   jmp     #table_end                 ' Skip over table
entry0  long    0
entry1  long    100
entry2  long    200
table_end
        mov     pa, entry0 + ($$ - entry0) ' Calculate relative offset
examples.description: PASM2: Using $$ for relative address calculation

examples.code:
DAT
        org
        
start   mov     pa, #$$ + 3                ' pa = address of 'start' + 3
        ' ...
examples.description: PASM2: $$ plus offset for forward reference

examples.code:
{Spin2_v50}
DAT
        org
        
        DITTO 8
        long    $$                         ' Generates: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7
        DITTO END
examples.description: V50+ DITTO: $$ as iteration index for simple sequence

examples.code:
{Spin2_v50}
DAT
        org
        
        DITTO 8
        long    $$ * 100                   ' Generates: 0, 100, 200, ..., 700
        DITTO END
examples.description: V50+ DITTO: $$ multiplied for scaled sequence

examples.code:
{Spin2_v50}
DAT
        org
        
        DITTO 4
        mov     reg + $$, #0               ' Clear reg+0, reg+1, reg+2, reg+3
        DITTO END
examples.description: V50+ DITTO: $$ for indexed register operations

examples.code:
{Spin2_v50}
DAT
        org
        
' Generate sine lookup table (0-90 degrees in 16 steps)
        DITTO 16
        long    round(sin(float($$) * PI / 30.0) * 65535.0)
        DITTO END
examples.description: V50+ DITTO: $$ in mathematical expressions for lookup tables

notes: In PASM2, $$ represents current cog address (not hub address)
Value is in cog longs (0-$1FF range for cog RAM)
V50+: Inside DITTO block, $$ becomes iteration index (0 to count-1)
V50+: DITTO usage requires {Spin2_v50} version directive
Context determines meaning - compiler resolves based on location
Single $ represents current hub address (different from $$)
error_messages: '$$' (DITTO index) is only allowed within a DITTO block, inside a DAT block
$$.oneliner: Current cog address (PASM2) or DITTO iteration index (V50+)

~~.description: Post-set operator - use value then set to -1
examples: value := ~~flag  // use flag then set to -1
